{{Short description|German biologist (born 1979)}}
'''Tobias J. Erb''' (born 9 May 1979 in Emmendingen<ref name="cv">[https://www.mpg.de/11384245/terrest_mikrobiologie_erb-tobias Erb, Tobias | Max-Planck-Gesellschaft]</ref>) is a German biologist and chemist who has been the Director of the [[Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology]] in Marburg since 2017. His research focuses on microbial biochemistry and [[synthetic biology]]. He is particularly focused on the fixation and conversion of the greenhouse gas CO<sub>2</sub>.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.mpi-marburg.mpg.de/erb/research-area | title=Research area }}</ref>

== Career ==
Erb studied chemistry and biology at the [[University of Freiburg]], where he graduated in 2005 with a diploma in biology and a master's degree in chemistry. From 2005 to 2009, he completed his doctoral thesis in microbiology at the University of Freiburg and [[Ohio State University]]. After his doctorate, he did postdoctoral research at the Carl R. Woese Institute for Genomic Biology at the University of Illinois from 2009 to 2011. From 2011 to 2014, Erb led a junior research group at [[ETH Zurich]]. In 2014, he moved to the [[Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology]] in Marburg as Max Planck Research Group Leader, where he was appointed Director in 2017.<ref name="cv"/> Since 2018, Erb has also been Professor of Biochemistry at the [[University of Marburg]].<ref name="y109">{{cite web | title=Tobias Erb | website=Philipps-Universität Marburg | url=https://www.uni-marburg.de/en/fb17/m4c/about-us/team/tobias-erb | access-date=11 December 2024}}</ref>

== Research ==
Erb's research focuses on microbial carbon metabolism, in particular the biochemistry and synthetic biology of carbon dioxide conversion. His research focuses on the discovery, function and design of novel enzymes for the conversion of carbon dioxide in bacteria, algae and plants, and their use for synthetic photosynthesis. In 2016, Erb and his team succeeded in realising the first engineered metabolic pathway for CO<sub>2</sub> fixation.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.mpg.de/14793996/kuenstliche-fotosynthese | title=Stoffwechsel 2.0 }}</ref> In 2020, his research team was able to demonstrate the first synthetic chloroplast.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.mpg.de/14788928/0506-terr-138345-photosynthesis-in-a-droplet | title=Photosynthesis in a droplet }}</ref> As part of a Max Planck research team, he was able to molecularly reconstruct the evolution of the [[Rubisco]] enzyme in 2022, using a combination of synthetic and evolutionary biology in the laboratory.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abq1416 | doi=10.1126/science.abq1416 | title=Evolution of increased complexity and specificity at the dawn of form I Rubiscos | date=2022 | last1=Schulz | first1=Luca | last2=Guo | first2=Zhijun | last3=Zarzycki | first3=Jan | last4=Steinchen | first4=Wieland | last5=Schuller | first5=Jan M. | last6=Heimerl | first6=Thomas | last7=Prinz | first7=Simone | last8=Mueller-Cajar | first8=Oliver | last9=Erb | first9=Tobias J. | last10=Hochberg | first10=Georg K. A. | journal=Science | volume=378 | issue=6616 | pages=155–160 | pmid=36227987 | bibcode=2022Sci...378..155S | url-access=subscription }}</ref>
